title: Separable Rank of Radial Kernels: Machine-Checked Characterization in Lean 4 and Applications
abstract: Filtering an image or three-dimensional wave field directly with a round (radially symmetric) kernel K(x) = phi(||x||^2) of width W costs W^d multiply-adds per output sample. When a 2-D kernel is a product h(x_0)v(x_1) of a horizontal and a vertical 1-D filter, it can instead be applied as two cheap 1-D passes; the separable rank R is the smallest number of such coordinate-product terms needed to sum to K. On a d-dimensional grid, rank R reduces W^d taps to d R W one-dimensional taps per sample (for example, a 9-tap-wide 3-D stencil drops from 9^3 = 729 taps to 3 x 4 x 9 = 108 taps when R = 4). Ordinary bell-shaped Gaussians exp(-alpha ||x||^2) have rank 1, but cannot form flat-top camera defocus disks or ringed wave stencils; practical designs therefore sum damped radial waves exp(-alpha ||x||^2) cos(omega ||x||^2 + theta) (complex-rate Gaussians), or more generally polynomials in s = ||x||^2 times real or complex exponentials (exponential polynomials). We determine which continuous radial kernels on R^d (d >= 2) have finite separable rank, and how many product terms each requires. First, K(x) = phi(||x||^2) has finite rank if and only if phi(s) (s >= 0) is a finite sum of exponential polynomials; conversely, decaying complex-rate Gaussians with one shared width and equally spaced frequencies can approximate any continuous radial kernel that fades to zero at large radius. Second, for a single complex-rate Gaussian in d dimensions, expanding real and imaginary parts naively takes 2^{d-1} real products (4 in 3-D), whereas an alternating angle-sampling identity achieves the exact minimum of d real products (3 in 3-D); multiplying by a degree-k polynomial in ||x||^2 adds (d - 1)k terms per real exponential and 2(d - 1)k terms per complex-conjugate pair. Third, allowing sequences of lower-rank kernels that converge uniformly on bounded regions (border rank) never lowers rank in 2-D, whereas in d >= 3 dimensions it strictly reduces the cost of polynomial-weighted profiles: for ||x||^2 cos(||x||^2) in 3-D, exact real rank is 7, limits of radial Gaussians take 6 terms, and general real separable limits take 5. All 32 mathematical theorems are verified by the Lean 4 computer proof assistant; we then test their concrete predictions on finite pixel/voxel grids and 16-bit hardware in reproducible (unverified) Python/Triton experiments: on an RTX 4070 Ti Super GPU, orthogonalizing 2-D filter terms cuts 16-bit floating-point (float16) rounding error on bright bokeh highlights from 7.9/255 to 0.31/255 (0.33 ms on a 1920 x 1080 image at R = 4), and exact 3-term-per-Gaussian 3-D acoustic stencils cut step time by 24% (1.51 ms vs. 1.98 ms on 256^3 voxels) while keeping directional wave-speed error below 0.2% in spatially varying media where global fast Fourier transforms (cuFFT) do not apply. Code, proofs, and data are public domain (CC0 1.0) at https://github.com/OlliNiemitalo/kernel-rank-lean.
